result:
On rainy afternoons, the public library feels like a small country with its own weather. Coats drip beside the entrance. The windows turn gray, and every lamp makes a circle of warmth on the tables. Nobody asks why you have come. You can read, think, apply for a job, or sit quietly until you are ready to go home.

I like the shelves near the back, where the books on gardening stand beside the books on astronomy. One promises that, with enough patience, a seed will open. The other says that the light reaching us tonight may have spent thousands of years on its way. Both seem like reasonable things to consider while rain taps against the glass.

A child nearby is learning to whisper. He points at a picture of a whale, forgets himself, and announces its name to the room. His father reminds him where they are, but several people look up and smile. The child tries the word again, softly this time, as though the whale has moved farther away.

Eventually the rain stops. Chairs scrape, bags zip, and people carry their chosen books toward the desk. Outside, buses hiss through puddles. I borrow a novel I may not finish and step into the damp evening.

On the walk home, I think about the child and his whale. I hope he keeps telling people what he finds, loudly now and then, even if someone asks him to lower his voice. I hope, too, that he always has a place to bring his questions when the weather turns bad.
